<a id="auto-size-mep"></a>

### Auto size MEP

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** size these ducts from the air they actually carry.

Sizes duct from the airflow it already carries, by the velocity method: required area is flow divided by the target velocity, snapped UP to the next real size. Reports the velocity that results and the aspect ratio, so an undersized run or a silly 6:1 flat duct is visible before anybody builds it. **The velocity is yours and no default is worth trusting.** A main at 7 m/s and a branch at 4 m/s are both normal and give completely different ducts for the same flow. Size one system at a time at the velocity that system is designed to. This fragment does not know which duct is a main and does not pretend to. **It reads the flow Revit already has, and does not calculate load.** Revit fills that in from the terminals downstream once the system is connected. A duct connected to nothing carries zero, and zero sizes to nothing - so zero-flow runs are reported as NO FLOW, never quietly sized to the smallest size in the list. A whole run with no flow is a CONNECTIVITY problem, and TRACE_CONNECTIVITY is where that goes. **It always rounds UP, never to nearest.** Rounding down to the nearer standard size pushes the velocity above the design figure, which is the one direction that causes noise complaints and rework. **Round or rectangular is a property of the duct, not a choice made here.** Setting a diameter on a rectangular type is refused by Revit. The shape is read per duct from the size parameters it actually has, and a duct whose shape cannot be read is reported rather than guessed at. **It sizes SEGMENTS, not a system.** It does not step a trunk down as branches take air off it - each duct is sized to its own flow. A trunk that should reduce at each takeoff has to be split first. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). There is no dry-run switch: previewing is the host's approval gate.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Kind** | Changes the model (`MODIFY`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **Works on** | what is selected in Revit: elements |
| **You say** | **target velocity** - a number - digits only - 250 or 250.5, not 250mm<br>**round sizes mm** - numbers - comma separated<br>**rect sizes mm** - numbers - comma separated<br>**hold width** - yes or no - true or false |
| **You get** | sized, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | none |
| **Capability** | `AUTO_SIZE_MEP` |

<a id="auto-size-pipe"></a>

### Auto size pipe

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-21 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** size these pipes from the flow they carry.

Sizes pipe from the flow it already carries, by the velocity method: the bore that gives flow divided by the target velocity, snapped UP to the next real size. Reports the velocity that results, so a run left screaming at 4 m/s is visible before anybody builds it. **NOMINAL SIZE IS NOT BORE, AND ON PIPE THAT IS AN ENGINEERING ERROR RATHER THAN A ROUNDING ONE.** This is the difference from AUTO_SIZE_MEP and the reason the two are not one fragment. A duct labelled 300 is 300 across the inside. A pipe labelled 50 has an internal bore of about 53 in steel and about 44 in a thick-walled plastic - and velocity goes as the square of it, so calling the label the bore is wrong by a fifth at the sizes where noise and erosion actually bite. **SO THE BORES ARE ASKED FOR SEPARATELY, PAIRED WITH THE LABELS.** Give both lists and every velocity reported is real. Give only the labels and the fragment still sizes, still reports - and says on every row that the velocity is approximate, plus which way it is wrong: a true bore LARGER than the label means the real velocity is lower than reported, which is safe, and a bore SMALLER than the label means it is higher, which is the direction that causes the noise complaint. An approximate number nobody flagged is the number that gets signed off. **THE VELOCITY IS YOURS AND NO DEFAULT IS WORTH TRUSTING.** A chilled water main at 2.5 m/s and a branch at 1.0 m/s are both normal and give completely different pipes for the same flow, and copper, steel and plastic have different erosion limits. Size one system at a time, at that system's figure. This fragment does not know what service it is looking at and does not pretend to. **IT READS THE FLOW REVIT ALREADY HAS AND CALCULATES NO DEMAND.** Revit fills that in from the fixtures and equipment downstream once the system is connected. A pipe connected to nothing reads zero, and zero sizes to nothing - so those are reported as NO FLOW, never quietly sized to the smallest pipe in the list. A whole run with no flow is a CONNECTIVITY problem and TRACE_CONNECTIVITY is where it goes. **IT IS NOT THE FIXTURE-UNIT SIZER AND IT IS NOT FOR DRAINAGE.** Domestic hot and cold water is sized from fixture units through a probable-demand curve, which takes completely different inputs; a gravity drain is sized on fixture units and fall, not on a velocity in a full bore. Both are different jobs, not different numbers in this one. **IT ALWAYS ROUNDS UP, NEVER TO NEAREST.** Rounding down to the nearer size pushes the velocity above the design figure, which is the one direction that causes noise and rework. **IT SIZES SEGMENTS, NOT A SYSTEM.** It does not step a main down as branches take flow off it - each pipe is sized to its own flow. A main that should reduce at each tee has to be split first. **EVERY SIZE IS READ BACK.** A pipe type whose segment offers only certain sizes refuses anything else, and it refuses quietly. The velocity reported is computed on the size that came back, not on the size that was asked for. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). There is no dry-run switch: previewing is the host's approval gate.

| **You get** | sized, findings, opened by resize |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |

<a id="cap-open-pipe-ends"></a>

### Cap open pipe ends

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** cap the open ends on these pipes.

Puts a cap fitting on every open end of the pipes given, sized to the pipe and connected to it. The termination a run drawn leg by leg never got. **THE SET IT IS GIVEN IS THE DECISION, AND THAT IS WHY THIS ONLY CAPS.** An open end is very often deliberate: a riser waiting for the level above, a run stopping at a future connection, a leg left for the contractor. Capping every open end in a model makes it LOOK finished and hides the gaps that are real, which is worse than the untidiness it fixed. So the sorting happens before this fragment - FIND_DEAD_ENDS separates the deliberate ends from the accidents and SELECT_BY_CONNECTION_STATUS narrows to open ones - and this one does the writing and nothing else. It carries no report-only mode because the report already exists elsewhere and two fragments answering the same question is how they drift apart. **REVIT PLACES THE CAP ITSELF, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE REASON THIS IS CHEAP.** `PlumbingUtils.PlaceCapOnOpenEnds` finds the fitting, sizes it to the pipe, works out which way the connector faces and joins it. By hand that is a family lookup, a direction calculation and an instance per end, and it is where the earlier attempt at this went wrong. **IT IS PIPES ONLY, AND THE SYMMETRICAL CALL FOR DUCT DOES NOT EXIST.** There is no mechanical-side equivalent that places a duct cap. Saying so here saves the search: a duct is capped by drawing the cap as part of the run. Anything in the set that is not a pipe is named rather than silently dropped. **AN EMPTY CAP TYPE MEANS REVIT CHOOSES FROM THE PIPE'S ROUTING PREFERENCES, AND A TYPE WITH NO CAP IN ITS PREFERENCES FAILS PER PIPE.** That failure is reported against the pipe rather than taken as a batch failure - REPORT_ROUTING_PREFERENCES is where the missing entry is found. **EVERY PIPE IS COUNTED BEFORE AND AFTER, AND THE NUMBER REPORTED IS ENDS, NOT PIPES.** A pipe open at both ends takes two caps, so a count of pipes understates the work by half on exactly the runs that most need looking at. A pipe that still reads open after the call is named in `stillOpen` - the call can return without raising and leave the end exactly as it was, and a count taken from "we called it" would report that pipe as terminated. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). Placing fittings raises Revit warnings on a real model; the transaction's owner decides how those are handled, which is why no failure-handling option is set here.

<a id="check-fixture-connectivity"></a>

### Check fixture connectivity

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-10 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** is every plumbing fixture actually plumbed, per service.

Checks that every plumbing fixture is actually plumbed - each of its connectors, cold, hot, sanitary and vent, either joined to the right kind of system or reported as missing. Covers the SUPPLY side and the DRAINAGE side together, because a fixture has both and checking one without the other passes half a defect. Read-only. **IT REPORTS BY SERVICE, WHICH IS THE ONLY USEFUL FORM.** *"Twelve fixtures have an unconnected connector"* is not actionable. *"Nine WCs have no vent and three basins have no hot water"* is. Every connector is classified by its own pipe system type and the table is one row per service per fixture. **A FIXTURE WITH NO CONNECTORS AT ALL IS A DIFFERENT DEFECT** from one with an unconnected service, and it is usually a family problem rather than a modelling one - the family was never built to be plumbed. Counted separately, because the fix is different and it is the row that keeps coming back until somebody looks at the family. **IT IS NOT `FIND_DEAD_ENDS` FROM THE OTHER END.** That one starts at open pipe ends and asks which are unexplained; a run ending AT a fixture counts as finished there and is correctly silent. This starts at the FIXTURE and asks which of its services were never run at all - a fixture nobody piped produces no open end to find, so the other fragment cannot see it. **THE SERVICE NAMES COME FROM REVIT'S OWN CLASSIFICATION**, not from the pipe system's name. A system somebody renamed still reports as sanitary or as domestic cold water, which is what makes the report comparable across projects.

<a id="check-flow-direction"></a>

### Check flow direction

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-10 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** joints where the flow contradicts itself - two outs meeting, or two ins.

Checks that the flow through a system agrees with itself. Every joined pair of connectors should be one **out** meeting one **in**. Two connectors both pushing out at the same joint, or both pulling in, is a system that cannot work as drawn. **IT IS INVISIBLE ON SCREEN AND THAT IS WHY IT NEEDS A CHECK.** The ducts touch, the fittings look right, the run reads as finished. Nothing about a contradictory joint draws differently, and Revit does not refuse it - it simply stops calculating sensible flow past that point, which is then blamed on the equipment. **IT IS THE OTHER HALF OF `TRACE_CONNECTIVITY`'s whole-set split** (FIND_SYSTEM_ISLANDS until 2026-11-01). That one asks whether the pieces are joined at all. This asks whether the joins make sense. A system can be perfectly whole and still have two pumps facing each other, and a connectivity check reports it as one healthy network. **BIDIRECTIONAL CONNECTORS ARE NOT A FAULT AND ARE NOT COUNTED.** Plenty of fittings and accessories carry them legitimately, and flagging them would fill the report with pairs nobody can act on - after which nobody reads it.

**"THE ARROWS ARE WRONG" MEANS TWO DIFFERENT JOBS AND ONE OF THEM CHANGES THE MODEL:** | What you meant | Use | |---|---| | "is the flow going the right way", "are the arrows pointing the right way" - to check | `CHECK_FLOW_DIRECTION`, read-only | | "the diffuser is the wrong way round", "turn it around" - to change | `FLIP_ELEMENTS`, which flips real elements | A question about direction must never flip anything. Both fragments carry this table - written one way it only routes whoever lands on the newer file. **IT REPORTS THE JOINT, NOT A VERDICT ON THE SYSTEM.** Which end is wrong is not something the geometry can settle: a reversed pump and a reversed branch produce the same contradictory joint. The pair is named and the fix is the modeller's call.

<a id="connect-air-terminals"></a>

### Connect air terminals

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).** Held on purpose: waiting on the owner's tolerance decision - how far Revit may move a terminal while connecting it before Heron calls it a problem - and on FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-187: on Revit 2024 this call lifted every terminal onto its duct's underside (550, 101.6 and 550 mm), made no tap, and joined a supply diffuser to a return duct, where the purpose above says Revit declines. The proof below records that very run; the owner signed it and chose to hold it, 2026-09-23.

**What it does:** tap these diffusers into the duct running past them, or pipe these sprinklers and fixtures to the main beside them.

Connects air terminals to the duct running past them. Revit cuts the tap into the duct, positions it under the terminal's connector and joins both ends - one call does the whole job. **This is the step after a terminal layout, and without it a layout ends as loose components.** Diffusers get placed in the right places and nothing has joined them to the ductwork; the drawing looks finished and the system carries no air. **It is a TAP, not a butt joint, and that is why it is not CONNECT_OPEN_ENDS.** That one joins two ends already at the same point and adds no fitting. This cuts a fitting INTO the side of a duct. A terminal sitting under a duct correctly does not pair in the other fragment, and correctly does tap here. **Nothing here moves a terminal, and Revit may.** Revit taps the duct at the point nearest the terminal's connector, so a terminal nowhere near the duct gives either a refusal or an absurdly long tap. The distance allowed is asked for, and it is the guard against both. The same call has been seen elsewhere lifting a terminal to meet its duct, so every terminal's position is read before and after and any change is reported in `moved` - how far is acceptable is not decided here. **Nearest is measured to the terminal's CONNECTOR, not to its insertion point.** A ceiling diffuser's connector is on top of it, and that is the end that has to reach the duct. Measuring from the middle of the diffuser picks the wrong duct in a ceiling with two running side by side. **A refusal is a bool, not an exception.** Revit returns false when it declines - a supply diffuser will not tap a return duct - and the model is unchanged for that terminal. Every false is reported by id and never counted as done. **A terminal already connected is skipped, not reconnected**, because reconnecting leaves the old tap behind as an orphan fitting. **Only a duct that fits is chosen, and joined means joined (version 3).** Only Air Terminals are tapped - equipment with a duct spigot is refused by name. The ducts are filtered first: a straight duct, not on the opposite air system (a supply diffuser never takes a return or exhaust duct), and then the nearest of those within the distance allowed - so a nearer return duct never hides the supply duct behind it, and one passed over is said by id. Whether a terminal or a head is connected is read off what is physically joined to its connector, never Revit's connected flag, both for the skip and after the tap; a terminal joined to anything but the duct chosen is refused, not counted. **Sprinklers and fixtures too (version 2, 2026-11-01).** CREATE_FIXTURE_BRANCHES was merged in. An element with a pipe connector and no duct one - a pendent sprinkler, a floor drain - is branched to the nearest straight PIPE among `ducts`: a riser from its connector to the main's centreline height and a level arm across to the main, at the connector's size, on the main's pipe type and system, joined at the head. The connector must face up or down and the main must be that way; the arm lands at least 100 mm or two main diameters in from a main's end; riser and arm together within maxDistanceMm. No fitting is made: `runs` holds the branches and the mains they land on, for FIT_MEP_JOINTS to make the elbows and the taps. A head whose branch Revit refuses, or that will not join, is taken back WHOLE - nothing is left for it, as nothing is left for a terminal Revit declines. Version 2's proof is owed; the card is DRAFT and the version 1 proof below is the record. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). Joining raises Revit warnings on a real model; how those are handled belongs to whoever owns the transaction.

This is the SECOND set, so `selected` is refused: the first set is what is selected<br>**max distance mm** - a number - digits only - 250 or 250.5, not 250mm |

<a id="connect-open-ends"></a>

### Connect open ends

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-10 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** these are touching but Revit does not think they are connected.

Joins pairs of OPEN connectors that are already at the same place - the cleanup for a run that looks continuous on screen and behaves as two separate systems. After a copy and paste, after a route drawn leg by leg, after binding a link. **It pairs on four tests and all four have to pass.** Distance alone produces nonsense: two pipes crossing at the same height have connectors near each other and must never be joined. A pair is offered only when both connectors are open, both are in the same domain (no duct joined to pipe), the sizes agree, and THEY FACE EACH OTHER. That last one is what separates a real end-to-end joint from a crossing, and it is the test the other three cannot stand in for. **It moves nothing.** Joining two connectors where they already are is the whole operation; nothing is dragged to close a gap. So the gap allowed is small on purpose - what it closes is a rounding-level gap, not a modelling error. Raising it to swallow a 200 mm hole produces a model that REPORTS as connected while the geometry still has a hole in it, which is worse than the problem it was hiding. **Each connector is used once.** Candidates are taken smallest-gap first and both ends struck off as a pair is taken - otherwise one open end where three pieces meet gets claimed twice and the second join throws. **This is not the tap job and not the stretch job.** An air terminal under a duct needs a tap cut into the duct's side, and two runs that genuinely end apart need moving or a new segment between them. Neither is this. A terminal sitting below a duct correctly does not pair here, and that is not a miss. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). Joining raises Revit warnings on a real model - the transaction's owner decides how those are handled, which is why no failure-handling option is set here.

<a id="copy-routing-preferences"></a>

### Copy routing preferences

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-16 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** give this pipe type the same fittings another one already uses.

Copies the fitting rules of one pipe or duct type onto another - the elbow, tee, cross, transition, union, joint and cap it inserts, with the size window each rule covers. The "make this type behave like that one" job, which SET_ROUTING_PREFERENCE cannot do because it replaces ONE rule and a group often holds several. **A GROUP HOLDS MORE THAN ONE RULE, AND THAT IS THE REASON THIS EXISTS.** A real copper type carries a full tee AND a reduced tee under Junctions, each covering different sizes. Replacing rule 0 leaves the second rule untouched and the type half-converted - which draws correctly until somebody reduces a branch. **SEGMENTS IS EXCLUDED UNLESS IT IS NAMED.** The segment carries the MATERIAL and the size table, so copying it silently replaces what a type is made of - and on a type somebody has just pointed at their own segment, that undoes the work without a word. Fittings are what "same fittings" means; material is a separate decision, and SET_ROUTING_PREFERENCE is where it is made. **EVERYTHING IS READ AND CHECKED BEFORE ANYTHING IS CLEARED.** A group is rebuilt by removing every rule and adding the new ones, so a failure halfway leaves it EMPTY - and an empty group inserts no fitting at all, with no error and no warning. So every source rule is resolved first, and a group whose parts cannot all be resolved is left exactly as it was. **A RULE POINTING AT AN UNLOADED FAMILY IS SKIPPED AND NAMED.** The source may carry a rule whose family is gone - a real case, seen on TCM_PIP_T031_Copper_Tee_Gas's MechanicalJoints. Copying that id would write a rule the target cannot use either, so it is reported rather than carried. **THE SIZE WINDOW TRAVELS WITH THE RULE.** A rebuilt rule with no criterion covers every size, and a size outside every rule's range gets NO fitting at all. Each criterion is read off the source rule and put on the new one, and the count is reported. **READ BACK, NEVER TRUST THE CALL.** AddRule returns nothing and throws nothing when a part is wrong for a group, so each group's rules are counted again afterwards and compared with what was asked for. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16), so copying every group is one undo entry.

<a id="create-hvac-zone"></a>

### Create HVAC zone

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** make an HVAC zone and put spaces in it.

Creates an HVAC Zone on a level and adds existing MEP Spaces to it - the grouping layer above Spaces that the load and airflow work depends on. **REVIT 2027 REMOVES THIS FROM THE API ALTOGETHER, AND THE FRAGMENT SAYS SO RATHER THAN FAILING TO COMPILE.** Both the zone-creation call and `Zone.AddSpaces` are gone from 2027's own assembly - checked there, not assumed. So both are reached BY NAME, which keeps ONE source compiling on all eight releases, working on 2020 through 2026, and reporting a plain reason on 2027 where the only route left is the Revit interface. Naming either call directly would break the 2027 build, and a try/catch does not help: it never gets to run. **A SPACE CAN BELONG TO ONLY ONE ZONE, AND REVIT MOVES IT WITHOUT ASKING.** A space already in another zone silently LEAVES that zone when added here. That is reported per space, because the damage is to a zone nobody was looking at. **THE ZONE AND ITS SPACES MUST SHARE A PHASE.** A mismatch is the usual reason a space is rejected, and it reads as the space being wrong rather than the phase. **A NEW ZONE REPORTS ZERO AREA, AND THAT NUMBER MUST NOT BE PASSED ON.** Revit computes it later. The space inside already knows its own area while the zone still says nothing - so the read-back here reports what was ADDED, never the zone's area, and anything wanting the area must ask again in a later call. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="create-mep-runs"></a>

### Create MEP runs

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** draw duct, pipe, cable tray or conduit - or a flexible duct or pipe - one run from here to there or every run of a layout, each at its own size, in one go.

Draws straight duct OR straight pipe - one run from here to there, or every main and every branch of a layout - in ONE call and ONE undo step, each run at its own size. Since 2026-11-01 it is the one straight-duct and straight-pipe tool: CREATE_DUCT, which drew one duct run per call, and CREATE_PIPE, which drew straight pipe between points, were merged into it. **Cable tray, conduit and flex too: the type decides (version 3, 2026-11-01).** CREATE_ELECTRICAL_RUN, which drew cable tray or conduit, and CREATE_FLEX_PIPE, which made one flexible duct or pipe, were merged in. A cable tray or conduit type draws containment between consecutive points and takes NO system type - one named with it is refused. A flex duct or flex pipe type makes ONE flexible curve through every point of a run, and needs a maximum length: `maxLengthMm` greater than zero, and a run whose route is longer is refused before anything is made. `runKind` - tray, conduit, duct, pipe, flex duct, flex pipe - may be said as well, and must then agree with the type. Sizes stay optional per run and read back: a tray is WxH, a conduit d25. **Duct or pipe: the type decides (version 2, 2026-11-01).** Name a duct type and a duct system and it draws duct; name a pipe type and a piping system and it draws pipe - as a flex type draws flex. The two must go together, checked by name before Revit is asked. A pipe run's size is a diameter, `d50`; a width by height on a pipe type is refused. Revit snaps a pipe size to its segment's sizes and still reports success - 77 asked, 80 made - so every size is read back, and a snap fails the whole job, named. **It exists because drawing was the slow half once the fittings were not.** On 2026-09-23 a five-room supply layout took twenty-five CREATE_DUCT calls and two SET_MEP_SIZE calls, then one FIT_MEP_JOINTS and one CONNECT_OPEN_ENDS. The owner asked for the drawing to be done at one time as well. With this the whole layout is three calls: draw, fit, join. **How to write the runs.** Runs are separated by | . Each is an optional size - WxH for rectangular, d250 for round, in millimetres - a colon, then the points in millimetres, x,y,z each, separated by ; . Consecutive points make one segment each. No size means the duct type's own: `850x195: 3075,-2100,3122.5; 3075,-1100,3122.5 | 300x300: 3075,-1100,3122.5; 3075,8100,3122.5` **One run is just its points**, with no size and no bar - two points give one duct, five give four, at the duct type's own size: `0,40000,2500; 3000,40000,2500` **It guesses no route.** Every point is given and used in order. Deciding where ducts go - reading the connectors, leaving room for an elbow or a transition - happens before this call. **It connects nothing.** The new ducts are left as `elements`, so FIT_MEP_JOINTS can take them straight from here, and CONNECT_OPEN_ENDS joins the free ends to equipment and terminals after that. **All or nothing.** A run it cannot read, a segment too short to exist, a duct Revit will not create, or a size the duct type snaps to something else - any one of them rolls the whole job back and names each problem (Article 8). ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| **You get** | elements, runs drawn, segments, sized, length mm, summary |

<a id="create-mep-system-type"></a>

### Create MEP system type

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** make a new duct or pipe system type.

Makes a new duct or pipe SYSTEM type - Supply Air, Chilled Water Return, Sanitary - by duplicating one that already exists and setting its abbreviation and its colour. **THERE IS NO CREATE CALL FOR A SYSTEM TYPE ON ANY RELEASE, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE SHAPE OF THIS FRAGMENT.** One is made by duplicating an existing one, checked against the reference assemblies at both ends. So the fragment's real job is choosing a sensible parent: the new type inherits its classification - supply, return, sanitary - from whatever it was copied from, and that classification cannot be changed afterwards. Copy a Return to make a Supply and it behaves as a Return forever, while reading correctly on every drawing. **IT IS NOT `DUPLICATE_TYPE`.** That duplicates the type behind the ELEMENTS handed to it - a duct's Duct Type, its size and shape. A system type is a different object: the thing that decides colour, abbreviation and which system a run belongs to. Asking for one and getting the other is the mis-route this closes. **THE ABBREVIATION IS WHAT APPEARS ON THE DRAWING**, in system names and tags, and Revit will accept a duplicate one without complaint - two systems then tag identically. Existing abbreviations are checked and a clash is reported. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="create-panel-schedules"></a>

### Create panel schedules

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** create a new panel schedule view for each distribution board that has none yet.

Creates the panel schedule VIEW for each distribution board handed in - the view Revit makes with Create Panel Schedules, which goes on a sheet. Until this fragment the library could READ the circuits (REPORT_PANEL_CIRCUITS) and make nothing a drawing could carry. **ONE SCHEDULE PER BOARD, SO ONE ALREADY THERE IS REPORTED, NOT DUPLICATED.** Every existing schedule view is read first and matched to its board; a board that has one is reported with that view and skipped. **THE TEMPLATE IS GIVEN, OR REVIT CHOOSES.** With `templateName` empty, Revit uses the default template for the board's configuration - branch, switchboard or data. A template that does not exist is refused before anything is made; a template of the wrong configuration is Revit's refusal, caught and reported for that board alone. **ONLY ELECTRICAL EQUIPMENT IS SCHEDULED.** Anything else handed in is listed and skipped, so a selection with a light fitting in it still schedules the boards. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION (Golden Rule 16). One operation is one undo entry, and the caller owns it.

<a id="create-parallel-runs"></a>

### Create parallel runs

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-13 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** make parallel copies of this connected pipe or conduit run, side by side or above or below it at a spacing, with the elbows re-made.

Revit's Parallel Pipes and Parallel Conduits: makes `count` copies of one connected run of pipes or of conduits, `spacingMm` apart centre to centre, to its left or right, to the north, south, east or west of it, or above or below it - the first copy one spacing from the run, the next two spacings. **Each piece moves perpendicular to itself and every bend is re-mitred**, so a copy on the inside of a bend is shorter and one on the outside longer, and every elbow, union and transition between the copy's pieces is made again on the original piece's own type, system, level and size. A plain copy moved by one distance is not a parallel run once the run bends - its leg running the same way as the move lands inside the original. **Left and right are looking along the run from its start** - its west end, or its south end when it runs north to south - and the reply names that point, so a copy on the wrong side is put right by saying the other word. **Never guessed.** The count and the spacing are asked for; a spacing not no wider than the run's largest pipe or conduit is refused, because the copies would sit inside one another. Only pipes, conduits and their fittings make a run: ducts are refused by name, and so is a valve or anything else in the run, which would be missing from every copy. A run that branches - a tee joining three of the pieces handed in - is refused, naming the tee. **The original is never touched**, and each copy's ends are left open. What can be known before drawing - the run, the values, an inside corner the spacing closes up - is refused with nothing made, saying why. A piece or a fitting Revit refuses, or a size the type snaps, takes the whole job back with Revit's own words, and nothing is kept (Article 8). The reply lists the new pieces and fittings of each copy. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| **You get** | copies, per copy |

<a id="create-pipe-segment"></a>

### Create pipe segment

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-16 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** make a new pipe segment, copying an existing size table and relabelling it.

Makes a new pipe segment - the thing that carries a pipe's MATERIAL and its SIZE TABLE - by copying the sizes of one that already exists, optionally relabelling every nominal size to its outside diameter, and optionally adding sizes the source did not have. **IT COPIES RATHER THAN INVENTS, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE DESIGN.** A wall thickness on a refrigerant line is a pressure rating. Typing one from memory into a size table is how a 40-bar line gets modelled as something thinner than it is, and nothing in Revit ever objects. The sizes here come off a segment a human already trusts, in Revit's own internal feet, never converted and never rounded on the way. **NOMINAL = OD IS A DECISION, NOT A DEFAULT.** Water tube is called by DN - a 15 mm tap connection on 12.7 mm pipe is correct and long-standing. Refrigerant tube is called by its OUTSIDE diameter - nobody orders "10 mm nominal", they order 3/8". A stock copper catalog carries imperial ODs under metric DN labels, so a half-inch refrigerant line tags as 15 mm. Passing nominalEqualsOd makes the label match the pipe; leaving it false keeps DN, and the answer says which was used because reading it off the result is the only way to be sure. **MATERIAL AND SCHEDULE ARE READ-ONLY ONCE CREATED.** `PipeSegment.Create` is the only place either can be set - there is no property to fix afterwards. A wrong material means deleting the segment and making it again, so the material is resolved BEFORE anything is created and a name that matches nothing stops the whole thing rather than creating a segment nobody wanted. **A SIZE NOT IN THE SIZE LISTS NEVER REACHES THE DROPDOWN.** The segment exists, the size table is full, and the pipe tool offers nothing. Every size is created usedInSizeLists AND usedInSizing, and the count of each is reported, because "created 17 sizes" and "17 sizes you can draw with" are different sentences. **REPLACE EXISTS BECAUSE A METRIC CATALOG SHARES NO SIZE WITH AN IMPERIAL ONE.** EN 12735 refrigerant tube is 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 28 mm OD; the stock copper catalog is 6.35, 9.52, 12.7, 15.88 - imperial, under metric labels. Adding the metric sizes to that table makes a segment offering both, which is honestly neither and lets somebody draw a 12 and a 12.7 in the same run. With replaceSizes the table is built from addSizes alone - and the source is still needed, because a segment must belong to a pipe SCHEDULE and the source's is the only one that cannot be wrong for a project already using it. **THE NEW SEGMENT IS EMPTY OF OPINIONS ABOUT WHICH TYPE USES IT.** Making a segment changes no pipe type. SET_ROUTING_PREFERENCE is the separate, deliberate act of pointing a type at it. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="disconnect-connectors"></a>

### Disconnect connectors

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-09 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** break the joint between these two, and leave everything else alone.

Breaks the physical connections BETWEEN the elements handed to it. Nothing is deleted, moved or resized - only the joint is undone. **IT DELETES NOTHING, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE.** Disconnecting an elbow leaves the elbow sitting there, connected to nothing. That looks untidy and it is the correct behaviour: deciding a fitting is now rubbish is a judgement about the design, and DELETE_ELEMENTS is where a judgement like that is made explicitly. A disconnect that silently swept up fittings would be a delete wearing a smaller word. **BY DEFAULT IT ONLY BREAKS JOINTS INSIDE THE SELECTION.** Given a duct and the fitting on its end, it separates those two and leaves the fitting's OTHER end attached to whatever is beyond. Breaking every connection an element has, including to things nobody selected, is a much larger act - it is available, but it is a flag the caller has to set, not the default. **A LOGICAL CONNECTION IS NOT A PHYSICAL ONE.** Revit's connector references include system membership as well as end-to-end joints. Only the physical ones are broken here; treating a system reference as a joint would quietly remove elements from their system and the drawing would not change to show it. **DISCONNECTING IS NOT A NO-OP ON THE SYSTEM.** Breaking a joint can split one system into two, or orphan the far side entirely. That is what was asked for, and it is reported rather than smoothed over - TRACE_CONNECTIVITY afterwards is what shows the shape that resulted. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION (Golden Rule 16). One operation is one undo entry, and the caller owns it.

<a id="draw-mep-from-cad"></a>

### Draw MEP from CAD

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** turn the duct and pipe linework of a linked CAD background into real ductwork or pipework in one go - the runs, their elbows and tees, at the dimensions handed in.

Turns the duct and pipe linework of a linked or imported CAD background into real Revit ducts or pipes, in one call and one undo. The geometry is taken from the CAD itself inside Revit, never estimated: the two parallel edges of a duct become one duct on their centreline, as wide as the gap between them; a lone edge becomes one pipe or duct. Broken pieces in one straight line are joined, and at each joint the fitting comes from the type's own routing preferences - an elbow at a corner, a tee at a branch off the side of a main, or a tap where the type prefers taps, a cross, a transition at a change of width. Each run takes the dimensions of the nearest hint handed in with a position; a run with none takes the default and is listed. A joint with too little room for its fitting is left unfitted and listed before Revit is asked; a failure Revit raises only as the call is kept still undoes the whole call. Arcs, splines, short pieces and blocks are counted and left out. The CAD file is left untouched.

|---|---|
| **Kind** | Changes the model (`MODIFY`) |

<a id="find-dead-ends"></a>

### Find dead ends

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** the runs that stop and serve nothing - the accidents, not the deliberate ends.

Finds runs that end at nothing - a duct stopping in mid-air, a branch left behind when the layout changed, a spur drawn to a terminal that was later deleted. **MOST OPEN ENDS ARE MEANT TO BE THERE, AND THAT IS WHY A RAW OPEN-END LIST GETS IGNORED.** A run ending at an air terminal, a fixture, a piece of equipment or a cap is finished, not broken. Report all of those as faults and the sweep gets switched off within a week. Every open end is classified first and only the unexplained ones are the finding: | Class | Meaning | |---|---| | `served` | the end sits at a terminal, fixture or equipment — fine | | `capped` | a cap fitting closes it — fine | | `stub` | very short and open — usually a deliberate future connection, reported quietly | | `deadEnd` | a real run ending at nothing — **this is the finding** | **"SERVES NOTHING" IS DECIDED BY WALKING, NOT BY LOOKING AT THE LAST ELEMENT.** A branch can end at a fitting that ends at another fitting that ends at nothing. Judging the last element alone calls that chain served, because a fitting is something. The walk follows the chain from each open end until it finds something served or runs out. **A STUB IS REPORTED SEPARATELY RATHER THAN SUPPRESSED.** A short open spur is usually deliberate and occasionally the whole problem. Folding it into `deadEnd` produces false alarms; dropping it hides a real one. It gets its own list and `stubLength` says what counted as short.

<a id="fit-mep-joints"></a>

### Fit MEP joints

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** put the fitting every joint in these runs calls for, all in one go.

Finds every point where two, three or four open duct or pipe ends meet among the runs handed in, and puts the fitting the geometry calls for at each one - elbow, tee, transition, union or cross - in ONE call and ONE undo step. **It exists because one-joint-per-call was the slow half of drawing a run.** On 2026-09-23 five rooms of supply duct took 25 quick CREATE_DUCT calls and then 90 calls for the fittings - a selection and a PLACE_MEP_FITTING for each of 45 joints - although every joint was fully known the moment the ducts were drawn. The owner's words: make the ducts, and then the path is known, so the fittings can be made at one time. **One joint or every joint - the same tool (version 3, 2026-11-01).** Hand in two runs and it fits the one joint between them; hand in a whole layout and it fits every joint among ALL the runs handed in. PLACE_MEP_FITTING, which fitted one joint a call, was merged into this card and is DEPRECATED. What it did that this did not is here now: two free ends of different runs that are APART are named with the gap - "two open ends 40 mm apart" - in `gaps`, and nothing is moved to close it; a run handed in with no open end is named in `noOpenEnd`; and when nothing at all is fitted, `refused` says why in that card's words - no duct or pipe given, no open end, the gap, or a single run whose ends meet nothing. Its two-to-four rule is a rule about one joint: a point where five or more ends meet fails the whole job. **The fitting is chosen as Revit chooses it**, and that is the rule Revit follows when one duct is dragged onto another: two ends at an angle make an elbow, two in line a union or - if the size changes - a transition, three a tee whose main is the most nearly head-on pair, four a cross. Nobody should have to name the fitting. **A branch drawn to the side of a main gets a TAP.** An end that lands on another run's axis, clear of both its ends, is joined with Revit's takeoff and the main is not cut - how a duct type whose routing preference is "Taps" wants its branches. The owner's correction, the same day: tap, not tee. Draw the main as one straight run and start each branch on its centreline; draw the main split at the branch points and three ends meet there, which is a tee. Which tap family is built is the duct type's routing preference. **Any other lone end is not a joint - unless the size changes at an outlet.** An end on a diffuser's neck, or on a unit's outlet of its own size, has nothing to fit, so it is counted in `freeEnds` and CONNECT_OPEN_ENDS joins it afterwards. An end on the open connector of a unit, terminal or accessory of a DIFFERENT size gets a transition, built into the duct and straight onto the outlet (version 2, 2026-09-28): draw the main from the outlet at its own size. A short outlet-sized piece before the transition, the way this was done until then, is what Revit's own Duct Sizing tore up - it deleted the main carrying the taps (FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-250). **All or nothing.** If any joint cannot be fitted the whole job is rolled back and every failed joint is named, with where it is and Revit's words (Article 8). A run with forty-four fittings of forty-five looks finished and carries no air past the gap. **Nothing is moved to close a gap.** Ends are grouped only when they already sit within the tolerance of one another. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="measure-available-fall"></a>

### Measure available fall

**DRAFT - runs in a chat, and its answer says so.** It changes nothing in the model, so it is not refused, but it has not been proved on a real model yet.

**What it does:** what fall can i get between these two points.

Works out what gradient a drain can be laid at between two elements - the question every below-ground and every long horizontal drainage run starts with, and the one that decides whether a layout is possible at all. **Asking it used to reach CREATE_GRID.** That was measured, and it is the shape of miss that matters: a drainage question answered by a fragment that draws a grid line. **It reports the fall three ways, because a drainage engineer uses all three.** The height difference in millimetres is what a level survey gives; the run length is what a plan gives; and the gradient as 1 in N is what a specification is written in. Reporting only one leaves the reader doing the arithmetic the question was about. **It says what IS available, never what is required.** Whether 1 in 80 is acceptable depends on the pipe size, the flow, the standard being worked to and the authority - and that judgement is not a fragment's. MEASURE_MEP_SLOPE reads the fall a pipe already has; this one measures the room to give it. **A rise is reported as a rise, not as a negative fall.** Water does not run uphill, and a layout where the second point is higher than the first is a finding rather than a number with a minus sign that somebody might use. **The run length is the horizontal distance, not the straight line.** A drain is laid to a gradient measured along the plan, and using the sloping length overstates the fall available - by little on a shallow run and by enough to matter on a steep one.

<a id="measure-fitting-area"></a>

### Measure fitting area

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-07 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** how much metal is in the bends and tees.

Measures the sheet area of MEP fittings - bends, tees, transitions, reducers, caps - from their own geometry, instead of estimating them as a percentage of the straight duct. Read-only. **THE OPEN ENDS ARE NOT METAL, AND SUBTRACTING THEM IS THE WHOLE TECHNIQUE.** A fitting's solid is closed: Revit caps it at each connector. Adding up every face therefore includes those end disks, where the duct carries on and there is no metal at all. Each connector's own opening is taken off - the circle on a round connector, the rectangle on a rectangular one. On a small elbow the caps are a large share of the surface and on a long transition they are almost none, so leaving them in does not inflate the total evenly: it biases the MIX, which is worse, because it survives a sense-check on the total. **A FITTING THAT COMES OUT NEGATIVE IS REPORTED, NOT SILENTLY FLOORED.** Where the openings exceed the surface - a solid that did not come through cleanly, or an oval connector, which has no simple opening area - the gross figure is kept and the id is named in `suspect`. A takeoff that quietly returns a nonsense area is worse than one that says which fittings it could not measure. **WHAT A FITTING IS COMES FROM ITS PART TYPE, NOT ITS NAME.** Elbow, Tee, Cross, Transition, Union, Cap: family names are whatever somebody typed, and the part type is what Revit itself routes on. It is reported per fitting so a takeoff can be read by kind - and unions, which are couplings carrying no sheet of their own, are named separately rather than dropped here. Whether a coupling belongs in a sheet-metal total is the estimator's call, not this fragment's. **THIS IS DEVELOPED SURFACE, NOT A CUTTING LIST.** No laps, seams, offcut or wastage - those are allowances a fabricator adds, and they belong wherever the caller keeps its own standards. Pair it with `REPORT_DUCT_WEIGHT` over the straight runs and drop any percentage uplift for fittings, or the same metal is counted twice. Areas are square feet, Revit's internal unit, per D-20. ASSUMES NOTHING ABOUT TRANSACTIONS - it opens none and needs none.

<a id="measure-mep-slope"></a>

### Measure MEP slope

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-08 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** what fall do these pipes have, and which are flatter than they should be.

The fall on each pipe or duct, as a percentage, measured from the geometry - and which of them are flatter than a minimum the caller states. Drainage that does not fall does not drain. It is one of the few MEP mistakes that looks completely correct in every view, passes every clash check, and is only found on site. **The slope is COMPUTED FROM THE ENDPOINTS, not read from the slope parameter,** and that is this repository's standing rule rather than a preference: Revit's own reported values describe intent and are not always the physical fact. A pipe whose slope parameter says 1% and whose two ends are at the same level is flat, and the geometry is the half that is true. The same reasoning found the real refrigerant pairing when the tags and the connector flags both said otherwise. **It answers "is there enough fall", NOT "does it fall the right way".** The sign it reports runs from the curve's start to its end, and Revit's curve direction is whichever way the modeller drew - two identical drains drawn from opposite ends report +1% and -1%. So the verdict is taken on the magnitude, and which end is downstream is TRACE_CONNECTIVITY's question. This limit was found by writing the negative case: the first version compared the signed value against a positive minimum, which would have failed a correct drain for the direction somebody dragged the mouse. **The minimum is a per-request input and has no default.** 1:100, 1:40 and 1% are different site answers to different pipe sizes and different authorities, and a number invented here would be a number quietly relied on. Nothing in this fragment knows what the job requires.

<a id="measure-mep-velocity"></a>

### Measure MEP velocity

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-08 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** how fast is the air moving in these ducts.

Air velocity in each duct, in metres per second, and which ones exceed a stated limit. The check behind *"is this duct too small for the flow"* — and before this fragment the search answered that with `CREATE_DUCT`. **It computes the velocity from flow and area AND reads Revit's own, then reports both.** Not belt and braces: Revit's velocity parameter is derived from the size and the flow it currently believes, and both can be stale — a duct resized after the system was last calculated reports the old figure and looks fine. Two numbers that disagree is the finding, not a nuisance. **The limit is a per-request input with no default.** 5 m/s in an occupied space, 8 or more in a riser, different again for a plant room and for a different authority. A number invented here would be a number quietly relied on across every project. **A round duct is not a rectangular one and the area is not the same arithmetic.** Both are handled; anything that is neither is named rather than guessed at.

<a id="measure-run-quantities"></a>

### Measure run quantities

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** how long each of these is and the total length - ducts, pipes, walls, beams - and how much metal is in a duct or pipe.

Reads the two numbers a takeoff is built from - each element's length, and for a duct or pipe its surface area - and says which elements had neither. Any element with a length: ducts, pipes, cable tray and conduit, walls, beams, lines. **THE LENGTHS IN MILLIMETRES AND THE TOTAL** (version 2, when MEASURE_ELEMENT_LENGTHS was merged in): `lengthsMm` for each element and `totalMm` for them all - "how many metres of duct is there", "what is the total length of wall". An element handed in twice is measured once, so the total and the list always agree. A length of zero is named in `lengthUnknown`, never added as nothing. This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code and is kept as a record, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again. **THE SURFACE AREA IS REVIT'S OWN, NOT ONE DERIVED HERE.** Revit already computes perimeter times length for a duct or pipe and keeps it on the element. For ductwork that number IS the sheet-metal area of the straight runs, so a takeoff does not have to be rebuilt from the size band - and where it is rebuilt anyway, the two are a free check on each other. **A MISSING AREA IS REPORTED AS MISSING, NEVER AS ZERO.** Cable tray and conduit carry no such parameter. Zero there reads as "no metal in it", which is a plausible number and a false one - the exact shape of failure this project is built around. `areaUnknown` names them instead. **IT MEASURES AND DOES NOT GROUP.** The question always arrives as "how many metres of each size", which sounds like one job and is two: read the numbers, then total them per group. `GROUP_AND_COUNT` does the second half for any quantity and any key, so the same totalling serves insulation, tray weight and concrete without being rewritten per material. Composed with `READ_ELEMENT_PARAMETERS` for the size, those three answer the takeoff question between them. **WHICH MEASURE TO TOTAL IS A REQUEST INPUT, NOT A GUESS.** "How much ductwork is there" means metres to one person and square metres to another, and picking a default would answer a question nobody asked. `measure` says which, and the chosen one is also handed back as `quantities` so `GROUP_AND_COUNT` can total it without knowing what it is - which is what lets the same totalling serve insulation, tray weight and concrete. Both measurements are still returned separately for a caller that wants both. **LENGTH COMES FROM THE PARAMETER, NOT FROM THE LOCATION CURVE.** They are not always the same number: a duct's curve is its centreline, and what Revit schedules is what a quantity surveyor is billed against. Reading the curve instead would produce a defensible figure that disagrees with the model's own schedule, which is worse than a wrong one because both sides look right. The curve is read only for an element that carries no length parameter at all - a beam, a line (version 2).

<a id="offset-mep-section"></a>

### Offset MEP section

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** lift or drop a stretch of this duct or pipe to go over or under something, with a leg at each end.

Takes one straight duct or pipe and moves the stretch between two distances along it up or down by an offset - to go over a beam, under a duct, round a clash - joining it back with a leg at each end, straight up and down or at 45 degrees. The coordination fix a modeller makes by hand most days. **IT BREAKS, MOVES AND DRAWS; FIT_MEP_JOINTS FITS.** The run is broken at the two points with Revit's own break, the middle piece is moved by the offset, and the two legs are drawn on the run's type, system and size. `runs` hands the five pieces to FIT_MEP_JOINTS, which puts the four elbows in and rolls everything back if one will not fit - the owner's order: draw, then fit. **THE FAR ENDS STAY WHERE THEY WERE, JOINED TO WHAT THEY WERE JOINED TO.** Only the stretch between the two points moves. The two breaks are made by Revit, which keeps the run's own end connections; the joints at the two points are opened, because a leg goes in there. **THE DISTANCES ARE FROM THE RUN'S OWN START**, as SPLIT_MEP_RUN measures them - whichever end it was modelled from. Both are refused when they fall outside the run, and the reply says where it ends so the number can be corrected. **A RISING OR VERTICAL RUN IS REFUSED** - up and down are the offset here, and a riser needs a sideways one this version does not make. Cable tray and conduit are refused: Revit gives no break for them. **AT 45 DEGREES EACH LEG RUNS AS FAR ALONG AS IT RISES**, so the stretch must exceed twice the offset, or it is refused. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION (Golden Rule 16). One operation is one undo entry, and the caller owns it.

Exactly one: none or several are refused, and so is a typed name, because an instance has no name of its own<br>**start mm** - a number - digits only - 250 or 250.5, not 250mm<br>**end mm** - a number - digits only - 250 or 250.5, not 250mm<br>**offset mm** - a number - digits only - 250 or 250.5, not 250mm<br>**angle degrees** - a number - digits only - 250 or 250.5, not 250mm |
| **You get** | runs, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |
| **Capability** | `OFFSET_MEP_SECTION` |

<a id="place-accessory-on-run"></a>

### Place accessory on run

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** put a damper in this duct and keep the run connected.

Inserts an accessory - a volume damper, a fire damper, a valve, a strainer - INTO an existing duct or pipe: the run is cut in two, the accessory is placed at the cut, and both halves are joined to it so the system stays continuous. **PLACING IT ON THE RUN AS A HOST DOES NOT BREAK THE RUN, AND NOTHING SAYS SO.** The obvious call takes the run as a host and looks exactly like the Revit command that does break it. It does not: the duct count stays the same, the accessory has no host, and it sits loose on top of the duct with neither connector joined - reported as a success. The correct sequence is to break the curve first, place the accessory, then connect each half's free end. **BREAKING SWAPS WHICH HALF KEEPS THE ID.** The original id stays with the SECOND half and the new id is the first. Anything remembering ids across the break is then holding the wrong element, which is why both halves are re-fetched by id rather than kept as objects. **THE TWO HALVES ARE NOT JOINED TO EACH OTHER BY THE BREAK.** That is what leaves room for the accessory. If the accessory fails to place, the run is left in two pieces - so a failure is reported per run with both ids, not swallowed. **THE ENDS ARE PAIRED BY SIDE, NEVER BY ORDER.** Which connector on the accessory faces which half depends on how the family was built and how the duct was drawn; the accessory is turned to the run, and each half's end at the cut is joined to the accessory end on that half's side. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16), so the break, the placement and both connections are one undo entry - which matters here more than usual, because a half-done insert leaves a severed system.

<a id="read-mep-system"></a>

### Read MEP system

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-07 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** what system are these on - name, type and abbreviation.

The system each element belongs to: the system name, the system type, and the abbreviation that ends up on the tag. **The system NAME and the system TYPE are different things and a modeller says "system" for both.** The type is Supply Air or Domestic Cold Water — the classification. The name is `SA 1` — the particular run. Two ducts can share a type and be on entirely separate systems, which is exactly the case somebody is checking when they ask. **An element with no system is a finding, not a blank.** A duct on no system is usually a duct that is not actually connected — which is the same defect `TRACE_CONNECTIVITY` exists for, arrived at from the data side rather than the geometry side. It is named, never left out.

<a id="read-space-loads"></a>

### Read space loads

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-14 (Revit 2020, 2024).

**What it does:** the heating and cooling load and the airflow on these spaces - typed, calculated and actual, and which have no design figure.

Reports each MEP Space's heating load, cooling load and supply airflow, and says for each figure whether Revit CALCULATED it or somebody typed it in. **Design and calculated are different numbers and Revit keeps both.** The calculated one comes from the heating and cooling analysis; the design one is what a person entered, and it overrides. A space where they disagree is either a deliberate design decision or an analysis nobody re-ran, and telling them apart is the whole value of reading this rather than reading one parameter. **A zero is not an answer, it is a question.** A space with no load usually means the analysis has never been run, or the space is unbounded and has no volume to load. Reporting `0 W` as a result would put a real number-shaped answer in front of somebody sizing equipment from it. **Typed, calculated and actual airflow, apart (version 2, 2026-11-01).** REPORT_SPACE_AIRFLOW was merged into this card and is DEPRECATED. Each space now also gives its SPECIFIED supply, return and exhaust airflow - what was typed - and its ACTUAL supply, return and exhaust, the sum Revit gives of what the space's terminals carry, in litres per second. `noDesignFigure` names the spaces with no typed airflow of any kind: zero against zero reads as balanced, and those are the rooms nobody has designed yet. A calculated supply is reported as calculated, in `calculatedSupplyLs`, and is never counted as the design target. `unplaced` names a space with no area - in the schedule, not in the model - and nothing is read from it. **It reads Spaces, not Rooms.** A Room carries no load - loads are the MEP half, and a model with rooms and no spaces answers nothing here. PLACE_ROOMS is what fixes that.

<a id="report-connector-loads"></a>

### Report connector loads

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-07 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** the engineering values Revit's system calculation actually runs on.

Reads what each element's connectors are CARRYING - assigned flow, demand, K-factor, fixture units, loss coefficient, pressure drop - and separates the zeros that are normal from the zeros that are a hole in the model. **THIS IS THE INPUT SIDE OF A CALCULATION EVERYONE READS THE OUTPUT OF.** Revit sizes systems and reports pressure loss from what is set on the connectors. A fixture with no demand, a sprinkler with no K-factor, an air terminal whose flow was never assigned - each contributes ZERO, and the system report then comes back clean, fast and completely wrong. The numbers look right because they ARE real numbers; they are the wrong ones. Nothing can tell from the output that an input was never filled in. **A ZERO IS NOT ALWAYS A FAULT, AND THAT IS WHY THEY ARE SPLIT.** A duct or pipe's own connectors carry no demand - the demand belongs to the fixture at the end of the run. So a zero on a curve is normal and a zero on a terminal, fixture or equipment connector is the thing to look at. Counting every zero as a problem produces a report nobody reads, which is the same outcome as not writing one. **READING A PROPERTY THE DOMAIN DOES NOT HAVE THROWS, IT DOES NOT RETURN ZERO.** A duct connector has no K-factor; an electrical connector has no flow. Revit raises. So every value is guarded on its own, and a value that is absent means "not applicable to this domain" - never "set to nothing". Guarding the whole connector in one block instead would lose the readable values alongside the inapplicable one, and report a filled-in fixture as empty. **WHAT IT DOES NOT ANSWER:** whether the values are RIGHT. It reports what is set. A flow of 50 l/s on a terminal that should carry 120 reads exactly like a correct one here.

<a id="report-connectors"></a>

### Report connectors

**DRAFT - runs in a chat, and its answer says so.** It changes nothing in the model, so it is not refused, but it has not been proved on a real model yet.

**What it does:** what connectors are on this thing, where they point, what is really plugged into them, and whether it matches - size, shape and domain.

Lists every MEP connector on the given elements - domain and, on a duct or pipe connector, its system classification (Supply Air, Return Air and the rest), shape, size, where it sits and which way it faces - and, for each one, the elements REALLY joined to it. Read-only. **THE WHOLE LIST ALSO COMES BACK AS ONE LINE OF TEXT**, `connectorSummary`, because a chat is sent only how many entries a dictionary holds: through a chat this answered `connectorFacts 1 entry(ies)` and nothing else (Project1, Revit 2024, 2026-09-23). It stops after 50 connectors, at a whole element, and says how many it left out. **`IsConnected` IS AN INTENT FLAG, NOT A FACT, AND IT HAS BEEN WRONG IN A REAL MODEL.** A connector can report `true` with nothing physically joined to it, and a run traced from that flag comes back complete while the air stops at a gap. So the flag is read and reported, and it is never what decides: the partners come from walking `AllRefs` and keeping only refs owned by ANOTHER element. Where the two disagree the element is named in `flagDisagrees`, which is the finding, not a footnote. **A SYSTEM IS NOT A PARTNER.** `AllRefs` also carries the logical MEP system the connector belongs to. Counting that as a connection makes every connector on a named system look joined, which is the exact failure the flag already causes - so refs owned by an `MEPSystem`, and refs back to the element itself, are dropped before anything is counted. **IT IS THE LOOK BEFORE THE DRAW.** Before a duct can be run off a spigot, four things have to be known and only one of them is in a schedule: is there a connector, what domain and size is it, which way does it face, and is it already taken. That is this fragment, and the direction is why it exists in geometry rather than as a count - a spigot facing into the wall is a different job from one facing the corridor. Positions and sizes are handed on in Revit's internal feet, not millimetres (D-20 keeps the conversion at the edge, where the user is). **VERSION 3 (2026-11-01): EVERY JOINT ON A PLACED FAMILY IS GRADED TOO** - CHECK_EQUIPMENT_CONNECTORS's job, merged here. On each family instance - equipment, terminal, fixture, fitting - every connector is compared with what is really joined to it: the *"the AHU has a 600x400 supply spigot and somebody ran 400x300 off it"* defect, which Revit builds with a transition and nobody sees until the airflow does not arrive. A pipe on a duct spigot is a DOMAIN MISMATCH, its own class - usually the wrong family was placed; a round-to-rectangular joint is a SHAPE CHANGE, said rather than measured; same shape is compared diameter to diameter, or width and height, within `sizeTolerance` in millimetres. `mismatched` names each element with a domain or size mismatch; `unconnectedSpigots` counts the spigots with nothing physically plugged in - usually the bigger finding, a gap no clash test and no connectivity walk flags. Sizes are what the FAMILY declares, and `findings` says so: check the first unit of each type against its datasheet once. The partner is the physical one the description uses - never the logical system, never the flag - which that card's grading did not do. ASSUMES NOTHING ABOUT TRANSACTIONS - it opens none and needs none.

<a id="report-duct-weight"></a>

### Report duct weight

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-08 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** how many kilos of sheet metal is in this ductwork.

Turns ductwork into a sheet-metal weight: the developed sheet area of each duct from its own shape, the metal thickness from a caller-supplied gauge table, and the kilos that follow. The procurement answer - *"how much ductwork is this"* - rather than the drawing answer. Read-only. **THE GAUGE TABLE AND THE DENSITY ARE THE CALLER'S, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE.** Which thickness a size gets is an office or project standard and it changes with the pressure class, the specification and the country; the density changes with the material. Building one table in would publish one office's standard as though it were a fact, and the number would then be quoted by people who never chose it. `sizeBandsMm` and `thicknessMm` are supplied as a pair - band `i` covers everything up to `sizeBandsMm[i]` - so the caller passes the table for the pressure class they are working to and the answer says which band each duct landed in. D-33: every number is a request input. **THE SHAPE IS ASKED, NOT INFERRED - AND AN OVAL IS WHY.** An oval duct carries a width, a height AND a diameter, so testing "has a diameter" calls every oval round and then uses the wrong perimeter. The duct type states its shape outright, so that is read first; the parameter pattern is kept only as a fallback for a duct whose type cannot be read, and every duct that used it is named in `shapeInferred`. An oval perimeter has no closed form, so it is approximated by the standard series rather than by pi times the mean of the sides, which is several percent out on a flat oval. **REVIT ALREADY KNOWS ONE OF THESE NUMBERS, SO THE ANSWER IS CHECKED FOR FREE.** Revit computes its own surface area for a duct - perimeter times length - and it is a genuinely independent second calculation of what is worked out here from the size. `areaDifference` is the gap between the two as a fraction. A disagreement is nearly always shape detection, and the weight is wrong by the same proportion, so a takeoff should be checked against it before anybody prices it. **FITTINGS ARE NOT IN THIS NUMBER AND ARE NOT ESTIMATED HERE.** A percentage uplift for bends and tees is a guess standing in for a measurement that `MEASURE_FITTING_AREA` now takes. Add that measured area rather than a percentage of this one, and no allowance is being counted twice. Areas are square feet - Revit's internal unit, per D-20 - and weights are kilograms, which Revit has no internal unit for. ASSUMES NOTHING ABOUT TRANSACTIONS - it opens none and needs none.

<a id="report-mep-pressure-drop"></a>

### Report MEP pressure drop

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-21 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** Revit's own pressure loss per section, and which sections are the index run.

Reads the pressure loss Revit has ALREADY CALCULATED for each duct or pipe system - section by section, with flow, velocity and friction - and marks the **critical path**, the index run that sizes the fan or the pump. It changes nothing. **REVIT ALREADY COMPUTES THIS AND NOTHING HERE WAS READING IT.** Once a system is connected and sized, Revit divides it into sections and works out the hydraulics for each. Every pressure question in this library was being answered from first principles while the model already knew. Measured before this batch, *"what is the pressure drop in this duct run"* resolved to `SET_MEP_SLOPE` - a **write**, for a question. **THE CRITICAL PATH IS THE POINT OF THE REPORT.** Total loss along the critical path is what the fan or pump has to overcome; the rest of the system is not the constraint. Sizing off the whole-system total instead over-specifies the plant. Those sections are marked, summed separately, and reported first. **A SYSTEM THAT IS NOT FULLY CONNECTED REPORTS ZERO, NOT AN ERROR, AND THAT IS THE TRAP.** Revit only computes hydraulics for a complete, sized, connected system. A run with an open end, an unconnected terminal or an unsized segment gives a section count of 0 - which reads as *"no pressure loss"* when it means *"not calculable"*. Those systems are listed **separately and named UNCALCULATED**, never folded into the table as zeros. `FIND_DEAD_ENDS` and `CONNECT_OPEN_ENDS` are what fix the cause. **SECTION INDEX AND SECTION NUMBER ARE NOT THE SAME THING.** `SectionsCount` bounds the INDEX; the number is a property of the section and is not guaranteed to run 1..N without gaps. Looping over numbers reads some sections twice and misses others - and being a report, it looks plausible either way. **This iterates by index and reads `.Number` off each section.** **PRESSURE AND FRICTION STAY IN REVIT'S INTERNAL UNITS AND ARE SAID TO BE.** Converting them needs the units API, which is the call that breaks at Revit 2021. A number converted by a guessed rule looks finished and is wrong; the raw value with its caveat does not. Compare against Revit's own system properties, where the same numbers appear formatted. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, every loaded link's duct and pipe systems are read the same way, and `linkedMatches` gives each link's calculated and UNCALCULATED counts and each calculated system's critical-path total - on a job split by trade the plumbing or mechanical model is often a link. `linksSearched` says how many links were read: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS CARRIED** - `systemsCalculated`, `uncalculated` and `criticalPathTotals` stay this model's own, so the host answer reads as before (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Only model elements are read from a link, never its views or sheets. Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer.

| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **You say** | **system name contains** - text<br>**include links** - yes or no - true or false; optional |
| **You get** | findings, uncalculated, critical path totals |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |
| **Capability** | `REPORT_MEP_PRESSURE_DROP` |

<a id="report-pipe-schedules"></a>

### Report pipe schedules

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-16 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** which pipe schedules this project has, and which segments are using each.

Lists every pipe schedule in the project and names the segments using each one. The question "is this schedule still needed" - asked before anybody removes one. **IT EXISTS BECAUSE CREATE_PIPE_SEGMENT MAKES SCHEDULES.** Revit keys a segment by its material AND its schedule together and refuses a pair already in use, so a second copper segment forces a NEW schedule into the project. That schedule outlives the segment: delete the segment and the schedule stays, in Revit's own settings, belonging to nothing. Making a thing nothing can list or remove is a gap, and this closes it. **NOTHING ELSE IN THE LIBRARY CAN REACH ONE.** A PipeScheduleType is an ElementType with NO CATEGORY, so FILTER_ELEMENTS_BY_CATEGORY and SELECT_TYPES both refuse it - correctly, since they are told to name a category and there is none. It never appears in a view either, so it cannot be clicked. Naming it here is the only route to one. **WHICH SEGMENTS USE IT IS THE WHOLE POINT.** A schedule still in use cannot be removed without taking a segment with it, and Revit does not warn first. Reporting the users by name turns "can I delete this" from a guess into a reading. **AN UNUSED SCHEDULE IS A REAL ANSWER, NOT AN EMPTY ONE.** `unused` is the finding somebody is asking for, so it is a result rather than a count of nothing found (D-52). Changes nothing and opens no transaction.

<a id="report-pipe-segments"></a>

### Report pipe segments

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-16 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** which pipe segments this project has, of what material, and in which sizes.

Lists every pipe segment in the project - its name, its material, how many sizes it carries and the outside-diameter range those sizes cover. The question "what am I allowed to build a pipe type out of", answered before anybody points a routing rule at one. **A SEGMENT IS WHERE A PIPE'S MATERIAL ACTUALLY LIVES.** A PipeType has no Material parameter - measured on Project1, 2026-09-15. It has a routing rule pointing at a segment, and the segment carries the material and the size table. So "which copper can I use" is this fragment, and SET_ROUTING_PREFERENCE is what then uses the answer. **THE SIZE RANGE IS THE POINT, NOT THE COUNT.** Refrigerant line sets are sized by imperial outside diameter - 6.35, 9.52, 12.7 mm - and water tube by metric DN - 15, 22, 28. Both are "copper" and a name cannot tell them apart. Reporting the OD range is what shows, at a glance, that a segment holds the wrong sizes for the job - which is a mistake that survives all the way to a material order. **THE NAMES COME BACK AS ONE STRING, DELIBERATELY.** A list is abbreviated to its first three entries by the time it reaches a reader, and a project with five copper segments then shows three - which reads as "there are three". One string is not abbreviated, so the answer is complete or it is obviously cut. Found by hitting it: five copper segments displayed as "Copper - A, Copper - B, Copper - C, ..." and the other two could not be discovered without guessing names one at a time. Changes nothing and opens no transaction.

<a id="report-routing-preferences"></a>

### Report routing preferences

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-16 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** which fitting this pipe or duct type will insert, and at which sizes.

Reads the routing preferences table off a pipe or duct TYPE - which elbow, tee, cross, transition, union and cap Revit will insert, and at which sizes. The answer to *"why did it put THAT fitting in"*. It changes nothing. IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE QUESTION WAS BEING ANSWERED BY `CREATE_MEP_SYSTEM_TYPE`. Measured before this batch, both *"report the routing preferences of this pipe type"* and *"which fittings does this pipe type use"* resolved there - a fragment that CREATES a system type, for a question about an existing one. **THE THING THAT MAKES A TYPE FAIL SILENTLY: A SIZE OUTSIDE EVERY RULE'S RANGE GETS NO FITTING AT ALL.** Each rule carries a minimum and maximum size. Draw at a size outside every window in a group and Revit inserts nothing - the run just stays unconnected at that junction, **with no error and no warning.** That gap is what this fragment is really for, so the covered size range per group is reported explicitly rather than left to be worked out from a table of numbers. **A RULE POINTING AT AN UNLOADED FAMILY LOOKS LIKE A BUG AND IS NOT.** The rule is fine; the family is gone from the project. Same visible symptom as an empty group - no fitting appears - and a completely different fix, so the two are reported separately. **AN EMPTY GROUP IS A REAL ANSWER.** A type with no cap rule cannot cap a run. Reporting only the groups that have rules hides exactly the group somebody is asking about when a run will not close. Routing preferences are invisible until something goes wrong, and then they are the whole explanation. Checking one before drawing with a type you did not build costs nothing; finding out afterwards costs a redraw.
