<a id="report-space-envelope"></a>

### Report space envelope

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** every MEP Space's walls, roofs, floors and windows - areas, facing and thermal values - for a load calculation.

Reads the take-off a building's heating and cooling loads are calculated from (docs/44 section 4): every MEP Space in the model - its number, name, level, zone, Space Type, floor area, volume and height - and every face that bounds it, from Revit's own spatial geometry: whether it is a wall, the top or the bottom, its area, the way it faces (its outward direction, which the brain turns to true north), what is on the other side - outside, another Space, an unconditioned space - and the windows, doors and curtain panels in it with their sizes. **For each type met it gives the thermal values Revit holds** - U-value, and for glass the SHGC - and a value Revit does not hold is reported missing, never 0. A window with no SHGC read as 0 loses all its sun without a word; the brain refuses that Space and names the type instead. **Once per model:** the site's latitude, longitude, time zone and elevation, the True North angle, and the units the model shows loads and airflow in - so the values written back later are in the model's own units. **It calculates nothing.** The loads are worked out by Heron's HVAC engine (heron_building_loads), never here. **Every Space, not the selection.** The question is about the whole building, and nothing is usually selected when it is asked. **Every face's outline, and where each window and door sits** - in metres, in the model's own coordinates - so the Companion's 3D view draws the very faces the loads were worked out from, for the modeller to check before anything is written back (docs/44 section 12). **Linked walls only when asked for (D-59).** In a federated model the walls are in the architect's link; with includeLinks set they are read from it, their types keyed by the link they come from. Otherwise such a face is "unknown" beyond, and a finding says the links were not read. **Why one string.** A fragment's list output reaches the caller as its first three names (FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-195), and a take-off needs every face. So it crosses as one JSON string, `takeoffJson`, format 1, as READ_ELEMENT_TABLE's table does.

<a id="report-sprinkler-layout-spaces"></a>

### Report sprinkler layout spaces

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-21 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** the rooms a sprinkler layout is made for - each room's outline and holes, its level, the ceilings over it, the sprinklers already on its level, and the sprinkler types loaded.

Reads what a sprinkler layout of a room needs (docs/47 section 3), for the Spaces or Rooms asked: each one's outline in plan (its largest boundary loop, tessellated, in metres) and its holes (every other loop - columns, shafts), how many of its edges are separation lines, its level with both of the level's elevations, its location point, the ceilings on its level whose plan extent holds that point with each one's height above the level, every sprinkler on its level inside its plan extent with its point and its Elevation from Level, and - once - every sprinkler type loaded, named `Family: Type`, with its family's placement type. **Which rooms.** `*` is the Spaces and Rooms selected now - only when the model read is the one in front. Otherwise UniqueIds separated by `;`, so the same rooms can be read again whatever is selected by then. One that matches nothing is a finding, never a guess. **The heads are found in plan.** Revit's IsPointInSpace and IsPointInRoom test a room's height too, and a head at the ceiling is often above it (NEEDS-CHECKING AJ5). So every sprinkler on the level inside the room's plan extent crosses, and the brain tests each against the outline itself. **It calculates nothing.** The layout, its check and which heads are in which room are the brain's (heron_sprinkler_layout, heron_fire). **Why one string.** A fragment's list output reaches the caller as its first three names (FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-195), so it crosses as one JSON string, `layoutJson`, format 1.

<a id="report-sprinkler-network"></a>

### Report sprinkler network

**DRAFT - runs in a chat, and its answer says so.** It changes nothing in the model, so it is not refused, but it has not been proved on a real model yet.

**What it does:** one fire protection piping system's pipes, fittings, valves and sprinklers, and which connector joins which - for a hydraulic calculation.

Reads the network a sprinkler system's hydraulic calculation is solved on (docs/46 section 3): one fire protection piping system - every pipe with its length, inside and nominal diameter; every fitting with its part type and angle; every valve; every sprinkler with the K-factor Revit holds, its level and the Space it sits in; the system's base equipment - and for every element, each piping connector's point, whether it is an End or a Curve (a tap part-way along a pipe), and which connectors it is joined to. **Which system.** A name in systemName wins. `*` means the system of what is selected - only when the model read is the one in front - else the only fire protection system in the model. With none chosen it reads no elements and lists the fire protection systems there are. **The K-factor is read, never trusted.** Revit's assigned K coefficient crosses raw, beside any K-Factor parameter as Revit displays it; the unit it is held in is not one Heron relies on, so the modeller confirms each type's K on the Companion. **The Spaces the heads sit in** (docs/46 section 13.2): each sprinkler carries its Space's id, and every Space a head of the system sits in is listed once with its number, name, level, area and its outline in plan - the first boundary loop, tessellated, in metres - for the spacing check. A Space whose boundary cannot be read is listed with no outline and a finding. **It calculates nothing and joins nothing.** Which connectors meet is Revit's answer; turning that into nodes, and the hydraulics, are the brain's (heron_sprinkler_takeoff, heron_fire). A connector joined to nothing is written as joined to nothing - an open end is a finding, never closed. **Why one string.** A fragment's list output reaches the caller as its first three names (FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-195), and a network needs every element. So it crosses as one JSON string, `networkJson`, format 1.

<a id="select-by-connection-status"></a>

### Select by connection status

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** which runs have a loose end, and which are fully joined.

Splits a duct, pipe or fitting category into what has at least one OPEN end and what is joined at every end - the cheap sweep behind "find the loose ends", run before a system is trusted. **It is a local check, not a trace.** It asks each element about its own connectors and walks nothing. A run whose every piece is joined to its neighbour passes here and can still lead nowhere - it can be a closed loop connected to no plant at all. TRACE_CONNECTIVITY follows the chain, and splits a whole set into its networks; this is the question that costs one pass and catches the commonest defect. **ASKING A CONNECTOR WHETHER IT IS CONNECTED CAN THROW, and that is not hypothetical.** A panelboard's connectors include surface ones, and reading connection status on those raises rather than returning false - measured on a panelboard with six connectors. So only END connectors are asked, which is also the only kind the question means: a surface connector has no end to leave open. Every read is guarded even so. **An element with NO connectors is neither open nor joined, and is counted separately.** A duct accessory modelled without connectors cannot answer the question at all, and putting it in either list would be an invention. A large count there usually means the category is wrong rather than the model. **A fitting is included and that is deliberate.** A run is only as connected as its fittings, and the elbow nobody joined is exactly what this is looking for. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, every loaded link is read too and `linksSearched` says how many were: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded", which is a different answer from host-only. The same end check runs in each link and its matches are counted per link in `linkedMatches`. **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS EVER SELECTED OR CARRIED** - `elements` stays this model's own; the chain revives ids against this model, and a linked id that happens to be in use here binds an unrelated element (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Kind** | Answers a question (`READ`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **You say** | **categories** - comma separated, resolved BY NAME in Revit; a name matching twice is refused<br>**want open ends** - yes or no - true or false<br>**include links** - yes or no - true or false; optional |
| **You get** | elements, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |
| **Capability** | `SELECT_BY_CONNECTION_STATUS` |

**How to use it**

1. Open the model in Revit and connect Heron: press **Heron** on the Heron tab, so its heron turns orange.
2. In a Claude chat, ask in your own words, for example *"find the loose ends"*. Say the values under **You say** in the same sentence.
3. Heron answers in the chat. Nothing in the model changes.

<a id="select-by-electrical-circuit"></a>

### Select by electrical circuit

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** everything wired onto one circuit, or onto every circuit of a kind.

Gathers the elements on electrical circuits, matched by the circuit's kind - power, lighting, data - or by its name, or both. With the kind "none" it gathers the opposite: the devices and fixtures with an electrical connector that no circuit carries (version 3). **This is a separate fragment from SELECT_BY_MEP_SYSTEM on purpose.** A duct or pipe system type is a document element with a name a project can change; an electrical circuit's type is a fixed enumeration in the API. They look like the same question in a modeller's words and they are read in genuinely different ways, so folding them together would mean one of the two reading through a mechanism that does not exist for it. **A CIRCUIT'S ELEMENTS ARE ITS LOADS, AND THE PANEL IS NOT AMONG THEM.** This was measured: a circuit plainly involving a receptacle and a panelboard reported ONE element. That is Revit being correct and easy to misread - everything downstream of the panel is on the circuit, the panel FEEDS it. So the panels are reported separately rather than left as an apparent omission, because "1 element on a circuit between two pieces of equipment" reads as a broken filter. **Kind and name both narrow, and asking for neither is refused.** Every circuit in a model is a legitimate answer to no filter at all, and it is almost never the question - a refusal costs one more sentence and saves reading a list of everything. **The kind is matched as text against the enumeration's own name**, so "power" finds `PowerCircuit`. That is what a modeller types, and the alternative is asking them to know the API's spelling. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as version 1 did. With it set, every loaded link's circuits are matched the same way, and `linkedMatches` gives each link's loads, circuits and the panels that feed them - the electrical model is often a link in the mechanical one. `linksSearched` says how many links were read: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS EVER SELECTED OR CARRIED** - `elements` and `panels` stay this model's own; the chain revives ids against this model, and a linked id that happens to be in use here binds an unrelated element (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Only model elements are read from a link, never its views or sheets. Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer.

|---|---|
| **Kind** | Answers a question (`READ`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **You say** | **circuit kind** - text<br>**circuit name** - text<br>**include links** - yes or no - true or false; optional |
| **You get** | elements, panels, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |
| **Capability** | `SELECT_BY_ELECTRICAL_CIRCUIT` |

<a id="select-by-insulation"></a>

### Select by insulation

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** which ducts and pipes are insulated, and which are still bare.

Splits a duct or pipe category into what has insulation applied and what is still bare - the sweep behind "which ducts still need insulating" and "show me what is already done". **It asks the insulation, not the duct.** A duct carries no reliable "am I insulated" parameter; the truth is a separate element that records which host it wraps. So this reads the wrappers and builds the set of hosts they name, which is the real relationship rather than a parameter that might have been filled in by hand. **The lookup is built once, not per element.** Asking each duct "is anything wrapping you" means a scan of the whole model per duct. Reading every wrapper once and collecting the hosts it names is the same answer for the cost of one pass, and on a real model that is the difference between a second and several minutes. **Lining is not insulation, and whether it counts is asked rather than assumed.** External thermal insulation and internal acoustic lining are different elements doing different jobs, and a modeller asking "which ducts are insulated" may mean either. The report always says which was counted, so two runs with different answers are not a contradiction. **A bare duct and a duct that cannot carry insulation look the same from a count.** Fittings, flex and equipment are in the same categories a modeller names, so the bare list is the honest answer to "what has nothing on it" and not a work list. Whether each one SHOULD be insulated is a judgement, and it is the modeller's. **LINKED MODELS ONLY WHEN ASKED (D-59).** Given `includeLinks`, each loaded link's insulation is read in that link and its insulated or bare count given per link in `linkedMatches`, and `linksSearched` says how many were read, 0 when none are loaded. Nothing from a link is ever selected.

| **You get** | elements, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |
| **Capability** | `SELECT_BY_INSULATION` |

<a id="select-by-mep-system"></a>

### Select by MEP system

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** every duct and pipe on one system, or on one kind of system.

Gathers the ducts, pipes and their fittings that belong to one MEP system - either one named run, or every run of one system type - as a set the next fragment can act on. **System NAME and system TYPE are different questions, and this fragment makes the caller say which.** The type is the classification: Supply Air, Domestic Cold Water, or whatever short code the project renamed it to. The name is the particular run: `SA 1`, `DXS 2`. Several separately named systems share one type, which is exactly the difference somebody is checking when they ask. Guessing between them would answer a different question than the one asked and look identical - the same decision READ_MEP_SYSTEM makes for a single element, and CREATE_MEP_RUNS makes between tray and conduit. **They are read from different parameters, and getting that wrong is silent.** The name is on `RBS_SYSTEM_NAME_PARAM`. The type is an ElementId-valued parameter pointing at the system type element, so it is read through its display name - which is where a project's short code actually lives. Reading the name parameter first and falling back to the type never reaches the fallback, because the name parameter is present on nearly every duct and pipe: the fragment then matches names while reporting types. **The four categories are gathered in ONE pass, not united.** Uniting four collectors is the obvious shape and it has a trap in it: `FilteredElementCollector.UnionWith` does not carry each side's own quick filters into the merged result, so an instances-only filter applied per side is silently lost and TYPE elements land in the answer beside real ones - measured at 52 returned where 4 were right, every extra one a type. Taking all four categories in a single multi-category filter cannot have the problem, so the knowledge is kept here and the hazard is not. **Matching is a contains, because that is how these are named.** A project types `DXS` and means every `DXS 1`, `DXS 2`, `DXS 3`. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, every loaded link is read too and `linksSearched` says how many were: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded", which is a different answer from host-only. The same system match runs on each link's own ducts and pipes, and its matches are counted per link in `linkedMatches`. **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS EVER SELECTED OR CARRIED** - `elements` stays this model's own; the chain revives ids against this model, and a linked id that happens to be in use here binds an unrelated element (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer.

| **You say** | **match on** - text<br>**system text** - text<br>**include links** - yes or no - true or false; optional |
| **You get** | elements, findings |

<a id="set-air-terminal-flow"></a>

### Set air terminal flow

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** set each air terminal's design flow, in L/s, from a file of ids and flows.

Sets the design flow on each air terminal handed in, from a file - the element id in the first column, the flow in litres per second in the second - in one undo. **NO WRITER COULD SET IT.** An air terminal carries TWO parameters called "Flow": the family's own, which the duct connector takes its flow from, and a built-in one Revit works out from the connector. On 2026-09-24, in Project1, 110 L/s was written by that name to one terminal, and the read-back, by the same name, said 235.0 L/s - the family's default. On 2026-09-25 that terminal's connector parameter already held 110. The value had landed, and the read-back had not shown it. A write by name cannot say what it did. D-54 s3 refuses a name that matches twice rather than choosing, and since row 5b-203 every writer that looks a name up refuses "Flow" on an air terminal, correctly. **SO THE PARAMETER IS FOUND THROUGH THE CONNECTOR, NEVER BY NAME.** The terminal's one duct connector names the family parameter its flow is tied to, and that parameter, matched by id, is written. A terminal with no duct connector, or two, or whose connector flow is tied to no parameter - a Flow Configuration of Calculated or System - is named in `noFlowParameter` and left alone. **EVERY ONE IS READ BACK** after one regeneration. One whose parameter does not hold the value is put back to what it held and named in `refused`. The built-in "Flow" is read as well, and a terminal where it still shows something else is named in `builtInDisagrees` - reported, not put back. It does not work out what the flow should be. Splitting a space's airflow across its terminals is the caller's arithmetic, and so is the file. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |
| **Capability** | `SET_AIR_TERMINAL_FLOW` |

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** put insulation on these ducts or pipes, at a stated thickness.

Adds insulation to ducts and pipes at a stated thickness, replacing whatever is there. **Insulation is the difference between a run that fits and one that does not.** A 400 mm duct with 50 mm insulation needs 500 mm of clear space, and the clash check that was run before the insulation went on is the one that said the ceiling void was fine. That is why this belongs beside `FIND_CLASHES` rather than in a corner of its own. **Duct and pipe insulation are different API types and this handles both**, because a modeller selects a run and does not sort it first. **Existing insulation is REPLACED, not added to.** Revit will happily carry two layers, and a duct wrapped twice reports a size nobody drew. The old is removed first, and the count reports what ended up on the element. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| **You get** | insulated, replaced |

<a id="set-mep-justification"></a>

### Set MEP justification

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** line these runs up on their tops instead of their centres.

Sets the horizontal and vertical justification that positions a duct or pipe within its own section - the setting that decides whether a run of changing sizes keeps its centres in line, its tops in line, or one side flat. **It is what "align the tops" actually means on MEP.** A 400 deep duct reducing to a 250 keeps its CENTRELINE by default, so the top steps up and the bottom steps down at the transition. Above a ceiling only the top matters, and a run set out on its centres loses headroom at every size change for no reason. ALIGN_ELEMENTS moves whole runs to a level; this decides where the pipe sits inside its own size. **The choice is set, as the dropdown sets it.** Revit shows justification as a choice - centre, top, bottom - and this sets that choice by the word Revit shows for it, never a guessed number. A run already at it is counted apart. **An element that carries neither choice is counted, not skipped.** Fittings, accessories and flex do not have them. A run that reports twelve set when nine could take the setting would leave three stepping and nothing saying which. **The value is read back after writing**, because a parameter that refuses returns without complaint on some element types. UNPROVEN AGAINST A MODEL. The two parameters were compiled on 2020 and on 2027, so they exist across the range; that changing them moves a run already drawn has NOT been watched here, and it is the first thing to check when a model is in front of somebody. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **Works on** | what is selected in Revit: elements |
| **You say** | **horizontal** - text; optional, left out means *leave*<br>**vertical** - text; optional, left out means *leave* |
| **You get** | set, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | none |
| **Capability** | `SET_MEP_JUSTIFICATION` |

Once it is proved, you will ask: *"line these runs up on their tops"* · *"keep the top flat through the reducer"* · *"set the justification on these ducts"*

<a id="set-mep-size"></a>

### Set MEP size

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** set the width, height or diameter on these MEP runs.

Sets duct or pipe size - width and height for rectangular, diameter for round - on elements that already exist, and reports what Revit actually stored. **Revit changes the number and says yes.** A size that is not in the type's size table is snapped to the nearest one that is: ask a run for 77 and it comes out 80, the set returns true, and nothing is thrown. Reporting the requested number as the result is how a schedule ends up disagreeing with the model, and nobody finds out until somebody measures. `snapped` is that case, carrying ids and what each one became. **The wrong size for the shape is skipped, not forced.** Width on a round duct and diameter on a rectangular one are simply not there, and that is reported rather than treated as a failure - it is usually the caller having one list of mixed shapes, which is a normal thing to have. It is separate from CREATE_MEP_RUNS on purpose: resizing duct that already exists is at least as common as sizing it at creation, and the snap check should have one home. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| **You get** | sized, snapped |

<a id="set-mep-slope"></a>

### Set MEP slope

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-10 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** put a fall on these pipes so they drain.

Puts a required fall onto pipe or duct runs - holds one end still and lifts or drops the other until the run sits at 1 in X. The fix for what MEASURE_MEP_SLOPE reports: a drainage line drawn flat, or at whatever fall the mouse happened to give it. **Which end stays put is a design decision and there is no safe default**, so it is asked for. On a drainage branch the end that stays is the one already set to a fixed invert - usually downstream at the manhole or the stack. `anchorEnd` takes "start", "end", "low" or "high"; "low" holds whichever end is currently lower, which is the one that usually matters on a drain. **It writes the LOCATION CURVE, not the Slope parameter.** On a plain pipe Revit's Slope is its own report of what the geometry is doing rather than a handle that drives it. So the curve is set, and the parameter is READ BACK and reported. The earlier library also wrote the parameter "so a schedule agrees with the model"; that is the wrong way round - a parameter written to disagree with the geometry is a lie a schedule then repeats. **A riser is never sloped.** The earlier library guarded this with a 300 mm minimum run, an arbitrary number that a near-vertical pipe walks straight past: a 2 m drop with 10 mm of horizontal run would be re-drawn 10 mm long and the pipe destroyed. The test here is geometric instead - a run that rises more than it runs is steeper than 45 degrees, is a riser or a drop, and is reported rather than touched. **Both ends connected usually means it cannot move**, and Revit will either refuse or drag the neighbour. Those runs are named and left alone; the caller deals with the fittings first. **Group members are refused before anything is attempted.** A move on a group member is silently ignored by Revit - no exception, no return value, no change - so counting that call as success is how a report says "sloped 12" over a model where nothing moved. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). There is no dry-run switch: previewing is the host's approval gate, not a flag inside a fragment.

| **You get** | sloped, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2024 |
| **Capability** | `SET_MEP_SLOPE` |

<a id="set-routing-preference"></a>

### Set routing preference

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-13 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** point this pipe or duct type's routing rule at a different segment or fitting.

Points one routing preference rule at a different part - the segment a pipe type is made of, or the elbow, tee, cross, transition, union, joint or cap it inserts. The write twin of REPORT_ROUTING_PREFERENCES, which could say what a type would place but never change it. **A PIPE TYPE'S MATERIAL IS NOT A PARAMETER ON THE TYPE**, and that is the job this exists for. `Material` is absent from a PipeType - measured on Project1, 2026-09-15 - because the material comes from the SEGMENT the Segments rule points at. "Make this type copper" is therefore this fragment with partName=the copper segment, and is reachable no other way. **THERE IS NO SetRule ON ANY RELEASE, AND MEPPartId IS READ-ONLY.** Changing which part a rule points at is RemoveRule then AddRule at the same index, so the rule is REBUILT rather than edited - and whatever is not copied across is silently gone. **THE SIZE WINDOW IS WHAT GETS LOST, AND LOSING IT IS WORSE THAN IT SOUNDS.** A rule carries its criteria separately from its part, so a rebuilt rule with no criterion covers every size. Where the old rule covered 15 to 50 mm that is not a smaller mistake than naming the wrong segment: a size outside every rule's range gets NO fitting at all, with no error and no warning - which is the exact gap REPORT_ROUTING_PREFERENCES was written to find. Every criterion is read off the old rule before it is removed and put back on the new one, and the count carried across is reported. **READ BACK, NEVER TRUST THE CALL.** AddRule returns nothing, and whether it throws when the part is wrong for the group is not measured, so the part id and the number of rules are read again afterwards and compared. That comparison is what separates a change from a clean return - the argument MOVE_ELEMENTS makes about a group member, applied to a rule. **A PART NAMED BUT NOT FOUND RETURNS THE NEAR MISSES.** "Copper" and "Copper - K" are different segments, and picking one for the caller is a confident wrong answer wearing a right one's clothes. FILTER_ELEMENTS_BY_CATEGORY refuses that guess for a category; this refuses it for a part. **EDITING A TYPE CHANGES EVERY ELEMENT OF THAT TYPE**, not only the ones handed in. Two pipes of one type are ONE type. That is Revit working correctly and it still surprises people, so types touched are counted separately from the elements given. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16), so changing several types is one undo entry.

| **You get** | rules changed, types touched, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |

<a id="split-mep-run"></a>

### Split MEP run

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-09 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** cut this duct or pipe in two at a measured distance along it.

Breaks a duct or a pipe into two at a distance measured from the start of the run, leaving both halves in place and connected to whatever they were connected to. **Named for what it can actually do.** *"Split this at the wall"* is asked of walls, floors and ducts alike, and only the MEP case has an API behind it - Revit exposes a break for ducts and for pipes and for nothing else. Calling this SPLIT_ELEMENT would promise a wall split that no release can perform, so a modeller would ask for it, get a refusal, and have no idea why. **The distance is measured from the element's own start, which is not always the end a person is looking at.** A duct's start is whichever end it was modelled from, and right-to-left is as normal as left-to-right. So a distance that lands outside the length is refused with the length reported, giving the number needed to correct it rather than just "no". **VERSION 2 ASKS WHETHER THE TWO HALVES CAME BACK JOINED TO EACH OTHER, AND JOINS THEM WHEN THEY DID NOT.** Version 1 broke the run and said nothing about the joint: the far ends keep their connections, which is what the sentence above describes, and the new joint in the middle is a different question. The earlier library measured the break leaving that joint OPEN and had to close it by hand - unverified here, which is why this reports what it found rather than asserting it. A run split into two pieces that nothing bridges looks perfect on screen and traces as two systems.

<a id="trace-connectivity"></a>

### Trace connectivity

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-16 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** walk a real system outward from one element and report what it reaches - or split the whole set into its separate networks and name the ones nothing feeds.

Walks a duct or pipe system outward from one element and reports what it ACTUALLY reaches - not what the system name says it reaches, and not what Connector.IsConnected says. Both of those have been wrong in real work, on the same model, at the same time: tag names implied one pairing and the flag reported nothing connected, end to end, while the pipework was plainly joined. So this fragment walks the declared connections AND checks geometry, and reports the difference as a number - `joinedByGeometry` is how often the flag was wrong. **Or the whole set, split into its networks (version 2, 2026-11-01).** FIND_SYSTEM_ISLANDS was merged in. Leave `start` out and the set handed in is partitioned instead of walked: how many separate networks it is really in, each one's size, and - the finding - which networks contain no equipment, so nothing feeds them. A system that looks like one network on screen is very often three, and a walk from inside the main run never learns the orphaned branch exists. The islands are Revit's OWN joins, inside the set; connector ends touching within the tolerance that Revit leaves open are counted in `joinedByGeometry` beside them and never merge two islands - the two answers are kept apart, never added into one count. The tolerance is an input and is never assumed (D-33). How close two connector ends have to be before they count as joined is a judgement about a particular model, and a number invented here would be a number tuned later.

| **You get** | reached, joined by geometry, island of, island sizes, sourceless |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2024 |
| **Capability** | `TRACE_CONNECTIVITY` |
